1:
The heading — the silent dove among them that are far off, a Michtam of David when the Philistines took him in Gath — draws more comment than the plea itself. Calvin sets it in the flight to Achish: driven from every hiding place, David was apprehended, escaped by feigning madness, and the psalm proves that faith was secretly in exercise even under that weakness. Fear compelled the artful device that saved his life at the cost of his dignity, and what the psalm records is the strenuous contest between faith and fear. Henry keeps the dove as a portrait: innocent and inoffensive, driven from the sanctuary, mourning in distant countries, yet silent — neither murmuring against God nor railing at the instruments of his trouble — and so a type of Christ dumb before the shearers and a pattern for Christians. Delitzsch treats the line as musical notation, taking the plural as either distant men or distant places, questioning the vowel-pointing, and rejecting the rendering dove of the people in the distance because that noun is unheard of in Hebrew; he prefers dove of the distant terebinths, and insists the preposition means after the tune of rather than concerning.

Clarke will have none of it. He canvasses the ancient versions, notes that one construes the title as a small band of men and the dove-word from a root meaning to oppress, and offers a prayer for himself and the oppressed band that shared his misfortunes in distant places — but then dismisses the whole enterprise: there is no end to conjectures, and all the titles in the book are not worth one hour's labour. Augustine goes the opposite way, reading the inscription as a doorway one pauses at before entering. At the end means Christ, since the end of the law is Christ for righteousness; and the people put far off from holy men are identified by another title altogether, the one written over the cross in Hebrew, Greek and Latin, confirmed as by three witnesses. Gill grounds the plea in the danger: David was in Goliath's own city, carrying the sword of the man he had killed, and could expect nothing from those whose tender mercies are cruel, so he pleads no merit but mercy. Spurgeon presses the logic — man has no mercy on me, therefore double thy mercy to me; if justice has let loose my enemies, let mercy shorten their chain.

Henry itemises the complaint: the enemies are many, barbarous, unanimous and subtle. Ravenous beasts do not prey on their own species, yet a bad man would devour a good one. Ellicott works the vocabulary instead, noting that the word for man is either mortal man or, contemptuously, a rabble, and that the root behind swallow up is unclear — the Greek reads trample on, one later version bruise or grind, and the sense of greedily devouring may have come by the same road that lets us speak of devouring a road at speed. The closing phrase of the second verse divides the readers sharply. Ellicott denies it is an address to God at all, taking it as an adverbial accusative meaning proudly; Clarke agrees it is no divine title but renders it from on high, that is, from the place of authority, Saul's court and cabinet. On the refrain, Gill and Wesley take praising his word as praising God for the promises of protection made to his people, Clarke reading the preposition as through God or by his help. Ellicott finds the text suspicious, prefers the Greek reading my words, and construes it as finding words to praise God in spite of every enemy. Spurgeon lets the fear stand: David saw the imminence of his peril and was afraid, yet fear and faith occupied his mind at once, and it is a blessed fear that drives a man to trust.
5:
To wrest words is to put them on the rack. Gill takes the verb from the shaping of the human body and applies it to speech forced into a shape it never had; the same root can mean to cause grief, so the line may equally read my words cause grief — to the enemies, since he had declared he would trust and not fear, or to himself. The Greek and Latin rendered it they cursed my words. Clarke is concrete: they were spies, collecting his sayings and twisting them by innuendo into treason against Saul. Ellicott notes the verb properly means afflict, so injure my cause is defensible, though torture my words is clear enough. Spurgeon makes it a law of persecution: a wolf can always find in a lamb's discourse a reason for eating him, and prayers are blasphemies read the wrong way upwards. No mixture of good tones the malice down: king, psalmist, father or sufferer, they saw him through coloured glass.

On the gathering and the ambush the readings converge. Spurgeon has firebrands burning fiercer for being pushed together, and cowards who wait for odds — men of malice are men of cowardice. Clarke sees cabals dressed up as justice and safety to the state, and objects that the translators have missed the word rendered soul — it means animal life, not the immortal spirit — more than any other word in either Testament. Wesley reads it plainly: having severally employed their thoughts, they meet to compare and execute them, and lurk to pry into his private actions. Ellicott prefers they set spies, and notes that marking his steps is literally watching his heels. The next verse opens a genuine puzzle. Clarke and Wesley read it as a question about the wicked — shall their dexterity in iniquity be the means of escape? Gill canvasses the alternative that the clause is the psalmist's own petition: deliver me because of their iniquity. Ellicott finds the literal wording by no means clear and the versions no help, gaining sense only by a slight change of reading: for iniquity thou wilt requite them. Spurgeon simply prays it: trip them up in their tricks, for what God often does we may safely ask him to do.

The counted wanderings draw the warmest writing. Gill rules out the reading that would make them sins, for those God keeps no account of — blotted out, cast behind his back, drowned in the sea — and takes them as the flights of a man hunted like a partridge on the mountains, twelve of which have been reckoned. Henry marks that David was not yet thirty and had already moved from his father's house to the court, the camp, and exile; God numbered every weary step, and does not cast from his care those whom men have cast out. The bottle and the book he reads as compassion and memory: tears sealed among God's treasures, which when opened will be vials of wrath upon the persecutors and consolation to the mourners — what was sown a tear will come up a pearl. Clarke hears an allusion to the ancient lachrymatories, phials of glass, pottery or agate in which tears for the dead were offered at the tomb. Ellicott denies the allusion outright, points to the wordplay between bottle and wandering, and prefers the singular in the sense of mental restlessness, the tossings to and fro of the mind. Delitzsch insists on what can actually be counted: not flight, which is not a numerable thing, but the unsettled life of a fugitive, measurable by its duration and its many temporary stays. Spurgeon also refuses the fashionable Roman phials for a robuster metaphor: such floods had David wept that a leathern bottle would scarce hold them. Wesley ends on the question the verse raises: why pray God to do what he has done already?
9:
The turn from complaint to confidence is made by prayer alone. Clarke reads it as cause and effect: the moment the enemies know he is calling on God, who will hear and save, they take flight — the cry of faith is more dreadful to spiritual foes than any war-cry to those it surprises. He grounds the certainty in memory rather than argument, having often had experience of the divine interposition: whoever has God with him need not fear the face of any adversary. Henry says the same with a soldier's economy: no other weapons than prayers and tears are needed, and the enemies against whom we fight best upon our knees are the spiritual ones. The refrain then returns, and Gill takes its repetition as deliberate — doubled for the greater certainty of the thing, and to show a fixed resolution and strong affection for God and his word. Henry glosses it as firm dependence on the promise for the sake of the one who made it: when we credit a man's bill we honour him that drew it, and to depend on the promise without staggering is itself to praise the word.

Spurgeon leaves the phrase deliberately open. It may mean that by God's grace he will praise God, in which case every emotion we direct towards God must also be produced by him; or that what in God is most the object of praise is his word and the faithfulness with which he keeps it, in which case our hearts should be attached to the sure word of promise and to the Word made flesh. He will not choose, but draws a rule from the ambiguity: praise never special in its direction cannot be very thoughtful, nor, it is to be feared, very acceptable. The shift to the covenant name in the second line marks a delight in God under every aspect, and the song is repeated because he loves to dwell on it. The vows that follow are read as an obligation of the same kind. Gill calls them debts, contracted in distress and now to be paid off, fresh in the memory when trouble is over and men commonly forget. Delitzsch renders the phrase as incumbent upon me, distinguishing the pledged vow-offering from the thank-offering and insisting neither will be wanting.

Henry refuses the idea of a weight: the vows are not a burden but a badge he glories in, not fetters that hamper him — such are superstitious vows — but a bridle restraining him from what would hurt and directing him in duty, and God is not merely a witness to them but a party. Clarke turns the verse on the reader, listing the renunciations every believer has already promised and asking bluntly whether he will pay them. Ellicott is the dissenting technician, observing that the possessive form behind thy vows, meaning vows made to thee, is most unusual. The closing verse divides on tense. Ellicott prefers hast thou not delivered to the received future, and notes that the word behind falling is literally a thrust. Clarke keeps the forward look, taking the deliverance as being kept from any false way and steadied in a godly course, and glosses the last phrase as pleasing God through the whole course of human life. Henry allows both readings at once — the words may be prayer pleading experience or praise raising expectation, since God has done the greater and will therefore do the less, having begun a good work he will perfect. Gill objects that the soul cannot die, being immortal, so the rescue must be of his person from imminent danger; but he then widens it to the spiritual death from which regenerating grace quickens, and to the eternal death from which the second death shall have no power to reclaim him.
